modules.title: 1.1 Anatomy of a Price Bar (The Building Block)

sections.heading: 1. The Four Pillars of Every Price Bar (OHLC)
sections.content: Every financial chart—whether a 2-minute E-mini futures chart or a daily stock chart—is composed of individual price bars. In Al Brooks price action, a bar is not merely a visual tick; it is a battleground between institutional buyers (bulls) and sellers (bears). Every bar contains four critical data points: Open, High, Low, and Close (OHLC).
sections.keyRule: The Close is universally considered the single most important data point on any chart. Where a bar closes tells you precisely who won the battle during that time period.

sections.heading: 2. Bar Psychology & Institutional Intent
sections.content: When a bar closes near its high (forming a bull trend bar), it proves that buyers were willing to accumulate inventory aggressively right up to the final second of the bar's timeframe. Institutions do not chase the market unless they have high conviction. Conversely, a bar closing near its low (a bear trend bar) shows aggressive selling dominance.

barBreakdownExample.scenario: A 5-minute ES bar opens at 5000, drops to an early low of 4995, and surges to close at 5012.
barBreakdownExample.psychology: The initial drop to 4995 traps early breakout shorts. When buyers step in and drive the price up to 5012, those trapped shorts are forced to buy back their positions to cut losses, creating fuel for the next bar.

sections.heading: 3. Tails and Wicks: The Footprint of Rejection
sections.content: Tails represent price extremes where one side attempted a breakout or directional push but was violently rebuffed by opposing participants. A long lower tail means bears pushed prices down, but buyers flooded the market with limit orders, creating immediate rejection and buying pressure.
sections.visualCue: Long lower tail = Bullish rejection / buying pressure. Long upper tail = Bearish rejection / selling pressure.

chartIllustration.title: Visual Breakdown: Bull Trend Bar vs. Bear Trend Bar
chartIllustration.description: Notice how the bull bar closes near its high with a small upper tail, whereas the bear bar closes near its low with a small lower tail.

sections.heading: 1. Defining Trend Momentum
sections.content: Bars fall into two core behavioral categories: Trend Bars and Dojis. A trend bar possesses a wide body (the distance between open and close) that takes up a dominant percentage of the total bar height, closing near its absolute extreme.
sections.keyRule: Consecutive trend bars with overlapping bodies indicate a 'Tight Channel'—one of the highest-probability momentum states in trading.

sections.heading: 2. The Anatomy of Equilibrium (Dojis)
sections.content: A doji occurs when the open and close are virtually identical. This represents absolute market equilibrium—neither bulls nor bears could maintain control. Clusters of dojis in a trend often signal exhaustion and an impending transition into a trading range.

barBreakdownExample.scenario: A doji forming at the top of an extended bull trend.
barBreakdownExample.psychology: Longs are taking profits, shorts are testing the waters, and institutional algorithms are pausing. It warns traders not to buy the breakout.

chartIllustration.title: Visual Breakdown: Doji Equilibrium vs. Trend Momentum
chartIllustration.description: Comparing a body-dominant trend bar against a center-locked doji bar.

flashcards.question: What is the single most important data point on any price bar?
flashcards.answer: The Close. It reveals who won the battle for control during that time period.

flashcards.question: What does a long lower tail on a bear bar signify?
flashcards.answer: Price rejection. Sellers drove the price down, but aggressive buyers stepped in near the low.
